implementation_notes: Delegates are the language's callback type - Action<T>, Func<T, TResult>, AsyncCallback - and a lambda or method group converts to them implicitly, so a deferred callback is just a parameter or a field of delegate type; the event keyword adds the classic registration structure (add/remove, several subscribers) on top of a multicast delegate. For asynchronous work the Task-based pattern usually replaces the raw completion callback: Task and await deliver the result, IProgress<T> reports progress, and TaskCompletionSource exposes a callback-based API as a task. Keep an explicit delegate or event where the callback fires more than once (progress, event streams), where several subscribers register, or where the API must stay allocation-free on an existing target.
pitfalls: Event subscriptions hold a strong reference from the publisher to the subscriber, so forgetting -= keeps the subscriber and its object graph alive for as long as the publisher lives.
An exception thrown by one subscriber propagates on the publisher's stack and stops the invocation list; multicast delegates give no per-subscriber isolation.
async void callbacks funnel exceptions into the synchronization context instead of returning them to the caller - use async Task where the caller can await.
A lambda added to a delegate in a loop closes over the loop variable (for loops copy only if you do it yourself), so all invocations may see the final value.
